reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A sporadic alpha-synucleinopathy combining autonomic failure with either parkinsonism (MSA-P) or cerebellar ataxia (MSA-C)
Prominent, early autonomic dysfunction such as orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention or incontinence, and erectile dysfunction is a defining feature
The parkinsonism is usually symmetric, rapidly progressive, and responds poorly or only briefly to dopaminergic therapy
MSA-C presents with gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, and eye movement abnormalities
Pyramidal signs, marked dysphonia or dysarthria, and inspiratory stridor may develop and stridor carries prognostic and airway significance
Early falls, antecollis (marked neck flexion), and cold, dusky hands can be supportive clinical clues
MRI may show putaminal, pontine (hot cross bun sign), or cerebellar atrophy
Distinguishing MSA from Parkinson disease rests on early severe autonomic failure, poor levodopa response, and cerebellar or pyramidal signs
reference.pathophysiology: MSA is characterised by abnormal aggregation of alpha-synuclein in oligodendrocytes as glial cytoplasmic inclusions, with associated neuronal loss and gliosis. Degeneration involves the striatonigral system (producing parkinsonism), the olivopontocerebellar system (producing ataxia), and central autonomic pathways including brainstem and intermediolateral spinal cord neurons (producing autonomic failure). The distribution of pathology determines whether the parkinsonian or cerebellar phenotype predominates, although most patients have overlapping features and prominent dysautonomia.
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain for putaminal, pontine, and cerebellar atrophy and the hot cross bun sign
Autonomic function testing including orthostatic blood pressure measurement
Assessment of bladder function and post-void residual volume
Trial of dopaminergic therapy to document the limited response
Sleep evaluation for stridor and REM sleep behaviour disorder
Exclusion of secondary causes of ataxia or parkinsonism
redFlags: Inspiratory stridor or sleep-related airway obstruction, which may cause sudden deterioration
Severe symptomatic orthostatic hypotension causing syncope and falls
Rapid progression with loss of mobility over a short period
reference.prognosis: MSA progresses faster than Parkinson disease, with loss of independent walking usually within a few years and median survival of roughly a decade; stridor, aspiration, and autonomic complications drive mortality.
pitfalls: Diagnosing Parkinson disease and missing early prominent autonomic failure
Overtreating with dopaminergic drugs despite poor benefit and worsening hypotension
Failing to recognise stridor as a potentially life-threatening sign
Overlooking urinary retention and its complications
Attributing early falls and ataxia to ageing rather than the disease
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; a supervised trial of levodopa is warranted since parkinsonism may respond briefly, though the response is usually poor and transient

Treat orthostatic hypotension with non-pharmacological measures (compression garments, head-up tilt of the bed, increased salt and fluid) and pressor agents such as fludrocortisone, midodrine or droxidopa
Manage the neurogenic bladder with intermittent catheterisation for retention and appropriate agents for detrusor overactivity, with monitoring of post-void residual volume

Address inspiratory stridor and respiratory compromise with sleep evaluation, continuous positive airway pressure and consideration of tracheostomy, as stridor carries airway and prognostic significance
Supportive multidisciplinary care with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy for dysarthria and dysphagia, and falls prevention
Manage REM sleep behaviour disorder and coexisting depression
Undertake early advance-care planning and involve palliative care given the rapid progression
